hints: Remember where a non-competitive inhibitor binds, at the allosteric site not the active site, and ask yourself if adding more substrate can push it off.
Think about what normally changes rate (more enzyme, more substrate up to a limit) and then add what changing the amount of inhibitor does to the number of working active sites.
walkthrough:
**Recall how non-competitive inhibition works**

Think of the inhibitor fitting into a different spot on the enzyme, the allosteric site. It changes the shape of the active site so substrate cannot fit properly.

Key rule: Adding more substrate does NOT remove it, but the inhibitor still leaves fewer working enzymes, so Vmax is lowered.

**Test each factor 1, 2 and 3**

1 enzyme concentration: More enzyme means more active sites available, so rate rises. This always matters.

2 inhibitor concentration: More inhibitor means more enzymes are switched off, so rate falls. This definitely matters.

3 substrate concentration: At low substrate, more collisions mean faster rate until all the still-working enzymes are saturated. So rate still rises with substrate, just to a lower maximum.

**Put it together**

All three change the rate, even with inhibitor present. That gives 1, 2 and 3, which is option A.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. Enzyme, inhibitor and substrate concentration all affect rate, substrate up to the new lower Vmax.
options.B: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 2 but wrongly leaves out 3, substrate still increases rate until saturation.
options.C: Misses a key point. It leaves out 2, but more inhibitor means fewer active enzymes and a slower rate.
options.D: Misses a key point. It leaves out 1, but more enzyme means more active sites and a faster rate.
